claims.text: Wear performance of HEA protective coatings is governed by their ability to form a stable, self-healing oxide layer during wear.
High configurational entropy promotes homogeneous elemental distribution in HEAs.
Homogeneous elemental distribution stabilizes formation of the protective oxide.
Reducing the concentration of a key oxidizing element such as Cr will degrade the protective oxide layer.
Degradation of the protective oxide layer will worsen wear resistance.
Cr or a similar oxide-forming element facilitates protective oxide formation in the proposed HEA coating.
Mechanical stress and thermal effects can promote oxidation during high-load sliding contact in ambient or mildly oxidizing atmospheres.
A nanostructured, coherent oxide layer forms on the coating surface during wear.
The wear-induced oxide layer is self-healing.
Uniformly distributed alloying elements facilitate rapid formation of a coherent oxide layer during mechanical wear.
The coherent oxide layer acts as a barrier that reduces surface degradation.
Reducing a critical oxidizer makes the oxide layer less stable and less continuous.
A less stable and less continuous oxide layer leads to increased wear damage.
Under identical oxidizing wear conditions, the unmodified coating will have a lower wear rate than the coating with reduced oxide-forming-element content.
The unmodified coating will form a more continuous oxide layer than the modified coating.
Oxide-mediated wear protection is expected to dominate under moderate-to-high temperature and stress when oxidation is active.
Oxide-mediated protection may not govern wear under extremely inert conditions or other environments where oxidation is suppressed.
